title: Ravangla vs Namchi: where to stay
meta_description: Ravangla or Namchi as your South Sikkim base? Altitude, weather, views, room prices, food and which sights are close, compared side by side for 2026.
summary: Stay in Namchi (1,315 m) for town comforts, lower prices, warmer nights and the Char Dham and Samdruptse sights. Stay in Ravangla (about 2,100 m) for mountain views, cool forest air, Buddha Park, Ralang and Temi. For two nights or more, split them: one in each, 26 km and an hour apart.

sections.heading: Two towns, one hour apart
paras: Namchi and Ravangla are the two bases most visitors use in Namchi district (South Sikkim), and they feel quite different even though only 26 km of road, about an hour by car, separates them. Namchi is the district headquarters: a proper hill town of offices, schools, a covered market, a stadium and a central plaza, sitting at about 1,315 m on a slope facing south-east. Ravangla, often spelt Rabongla, is a small ridge town at about 2,100 m, on the saddle between Maenam and Tendong hills, built around one market street, monasteries and a growing ring of hotels facing the snow peaks.

The choice matters more than it seems, because 800 m of altitude changes the temperature, the views, the food on offer and how far you are from each set of sights. Below is how we decide for our own guests.

sections.heading: Choose Namchi if
paras: You want a town that works like a town. Namchi has ATMs, pharmacies, a district hospital, a covered market and plenty of places to eat, from momo counters and Nepali thali joints to bakeries and cafés around the central plaza. It is the better base for seniors who want medical help close by, for families who want evenings in a lit public space, and for anyone on a tight budget, because competition keeps room rates low.

Namchi is also the right base for the Hindu pilgrim circuit. Char Dham on Solophok hill is about 5 km from the bazaar and best at 8 am, so sleeping in Namchi or at the pilgrim lodge on the hill saves an early drive. Samdruptse and the Rock Garden are on the ridge road above town. Being lower and nearer the plains, Namchi is also an hour closer to Siliguri, which matters on the day you fly out of Bagdogra.
The trade-off: most Namchi rooms look at town and hills rather than snow peaks, and in May and June the afternoons can be warm and hazy.
list: Best for: pilgrims, seniors, budget travellers, short trips from Siliguri

Real options include Hotel Samdruptse in town, Seven Hill Resort at Phalidara above Namchi and the Sobralia resort (formerly Summit Sobralia) on the Char Dham road; there are many simple family-run hotels near the market

sections.heading: Choose Ravangla if
paras: You came to the mountains for mountains. Ravangla's ridge looks straight across the Rangeet valley to the Kangchenjunga range, and on a clear October or March morning the view from a good hotel balcony is the main reason to be here. The air is cool even in May, the forest of Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary starts at the edge of town, and the evenings are quiet, with mist coming up the slopes and prayer flags on the ridge.

Ravangla puts you closest to the Buddhist sites and the walks. Buddha Park is a 15-minute stroll from the market, Ralang Monastery is about 6 km down the road, the Temi Tea Garden about 20 km, Borong and its hot spring about 17 km, and the trailheads for Tendong and Maenam hills are within a short drive. Homestays in the villages around it, Kewzing and Yangang among them, are the best value in the district.
The trade-offs: fewer restaurants, a smaller market, colder nights between December and February, and rooms with the best views go first in October, so book early.
list: Best for: couples, photographers, walkers, birders, anyone combining South and West Sikkim
Real options range from backpacker favourites such as Hotel 10Zing on the market street to Mt Narsing Village Resort, a cottage resort about 3 km out of town

sections.heading: Why we usually split the nights
paras: For a trip of three nights or more in the south, we nearly always suggest one or two nights in Namchi and one or two in Ravangla. The sights divide neatly: Namchi's face east and are best in morning light; Ravangla's are best in the afternoon and at dawn for the views. Splitting also keeps each day's driving short. A typical pattern is Siliguri to Namchi on day one (3.5 to 4 hours), Namchi sights and a one-hour drive up to Ravangla on day two, Ravangla, Ralang and Temi on day three, and onward to Pelling (about 2 hours via Legship) or Gangtok (about 3 hours) on day four.

If you have only two nights and can only pick one base, choose by your main interest: temples and comfort, Namchi; mountains and monasteries, Ravangla. Either way, the other town is an easy half-day trip.

sections.heading: Evenings, food and getting around
paras: Evenings are where the two towns differ most. Namchi's central plaza fills after dark with families, students and snack stalls, and you can walk to a dozen places to eat: Nepali thalis, momos and thukpa, Tibetan-style shaphaley, North Indian vegetarian food for pilgrims, and bakeries with decent coffee. Ravangla shuts early. By 8 pm most of the market street is closed, and dinner is usually at your hotel or one of a few small restaurants near the taxi stand, so ask what the kitchen serves before you book.

Getting around is easier from Namchi too. It is a jeep hub, with shared vehicles to Ravangla, Jorethang, Gangtok and Siliguri through the morning, and plenty of local taxis for half-day sightseeing. Ravangla has a taxi stand and shared jeeps to Namchi, Gangtok, Pelling and Siliguri, but fewer departures after midday. If you travel without a private car, Namchi gives you more options when plans change.

sections.heading: Where else to stay in the south
paras: Three other kinds of stay are worth knowing. Homestay villages such as Kewzing, Yangang and Borong give you a family's home, home-grown food and village walks for about ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night with meals. Temi, around the tea estate, has a handful of resorts and the estate guest house, ideal for one quiet night. Jorethang, the low, warm market town on the Rangeet at about 500 m, is only useful as a transit stop, though it has decent budget hotels if you arrive late from Siliguri.

At the top end, South Sikkim has fewer luxury hotels than Gangtok or Pelling. Our premium South Sikkim trips use the best resorts at Ravangla, Namchi and Temi with private SUVs and add a night or two at Gangtok or Pelling's top hotels.

sections.heading: Booking tips for both towns
paras: October, the first half of November, late March to May, and the Durga Puja and Diwali holidays are peak weeks; book view rooms four to six weeks ahead. December to February and the monsoon months are quiet, and walk-in discounts of 20 to 40 percent are common.

Ask three questions before you pay: does the room face the mountains or the road; is there a heater or extra blankets in winter (Ravangla nights drop near freezing); and is the ₹50 per person state fee included. Hotels collect that Tourism Sustainable Development fee at check-in, valid for 30 days across Sikkim. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Ravangla or Namchi better for a first visit?
faqs.a: For views and mountain air, Ravangla. For comfort, food choice and lower prices, Namchi. Most first-timers enjoy one night in each, because the towns are only 26 km and about an hour apart, and their sights divide neatly between them. If you must choose one, pick by interest: temples, Namchi; monasteries and mountains, Ravangla.

faqs.q: Which is colder, Ravangla or Namchi?
faqs.a: Ravangla, by a clear margin. At about 2,100 m it runs 5–7 °C colder than Namchi at 1,315 m. January nights in Ravangla are near freezing with frost; Namchi stays around 4–8 °C. In May, Ravangla is pleasantly cool while Namchi afternoons can be warm.

faqs.q: Can you see Kangchenjunga from Ravangla?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days. Ravangla looks across the Rangeet valley to the Kangchenjunga range, and many hotels have view rooms. The clearest months are October to December and March to April, mostly in the early morning before cloud builds. From Namchi the snow views are partial.

faqs.q: How far is Ravangla from Namchi?
faqs.a: About 26 km by road, roughly an hour by car, via Damthang. Shared jeeps run between the towns through the day for about ₹80–120 a seat, and a reserved small car costs about ₹1,200–1,500 one way. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which is better for senior citizens?
faqs.a: Namchi is easier for most seniors: lower altitude, milder nights, a district hospital, pharmacies and level areas around the central plaza. Ravangla is fine for healthy seniors, but nights are cold in winter. Both are well below the altitude where most people feel any effects.

faqs.q: Where should I stay for Char Dham?
faqs.a: In Namchi town or at the pilgrim lodge on Solophok hill, about 5 km from the bazaar. Char Dham is best at opening time, around 8 am, so sleeping close saves an early drive. Ravangla is an hour away, which makes a dawn visit harder.

faqs.q: Are there luxury hotels in Ravangla or Namchi?
faqs.a: South Sikkim has fewer luxury hotels than Gangtok or Pelling. There are good comfort-class resorts in Namchi, Ravangla and near Temi. Our premium South Sikkim trips use the best of these and pair them with top hotels in Gangtok or Pelling for a night or two.

faqs.q: What do hotel rooms cost in Ravangla?
faqs.a: Indicatively, budget doubles cost about ₹1,500–2,500 and mid-range rooms with views about ₹3,500–6,500 a night in season. Prices drop 20–40 percent from December to February and in the monsoon. Homestays nearby charge about ₹1,200–2,000 per person with meals.

faqs.q: Is Jorethang a good place to stay?
faqs.a: Only as a transit stop. Jorethang is a warm market town on the Rangeet at about 500 m with useful budget hotels and jeep connections to Pelling, Namchi and Siliguri, but it has few sights of its own. Namchi is 40 minutes up the hill and a far better base.
